stem: What is the output of the following code?
code:
class Car:
    def __init__(self, brand):
        self.brand = brand

c1 = Car('Fiat')
c2 = Car('Opel')
c1.brand = 'Tesla'
print(c2.brand)
explanation: Each instance gets its own `brand` attribute from `__init__`. Rebinding `c1.brand` changes only the object c1; c2 keeps 'Opel'.

distractor_notes.b: Instance attributes belong to one object; changing c1 does not touch c2.
distractor_notes.c: 'Fiat' was c1's initial brand, never c2's.
distractor_notes.a: `brand` is created by `__init__`, so every Car has it.

stem: What will be the output of the code?
code:
class Book:
    def __init__(self, title):
        self.title = title

b1 = Book('Dune')
b2 = Book('Emma')
b1.pages = 412
print(b1.pages)
print(b2.pages)
explanation: `b1.pages = 412` adds an attribute to the object b1 only. b2 never got a `pages` attribute and the class does not define one, so `b2.pages` raises AttributeError after 412 has been printed.

distractor_notes.a: Adding an attribute to one instance does not add it to the class or to the other instances.
distractor_notes.b: A missing attribute raises AttributeError; it never defaults to None.
distractor_notes.d: `b1.pages` exists, so the first print succeeds before the error.

stem: What is the output of the following code?
code:
class Robot:
    pass

r = Robot()
print(type(r).__name__, isinstance(r, Robot))
explanation: Calling a class creates an instance of it, even when the class body is just `pass`. `type(r)` is the class Robot (its name is 'Robot') and `isinstance(r, Robot)` is True.

distractor_notes.b: type() returns the most specific class of the object, not its base class `object`.
distractor_notes.d: `type` is the class of classes (that is `type(Robot)`), not the class of r.
distractor_notes.a: r was created by `Robot()`, so it is an instance of Robot.
